title: Detection of Email Accounts
summary: This detection strategy covers compromise of email accounts used as infrastructure, whether the account belongs to your organisation or to a supplier that your staff already trust. A taken over mailbox lets an attacker read message history, send believable requests and trigger password resets on other services. The telemetry that makes it visible is mail service sign in and audit logging, mailbox rule and forwarding changes, message trace records for outbound volume and identity protection alerts for risky sign in. It fails because the attacker often signs in with valid credentials from a residential address, so the event looks like an ordinary user working from a new place.

beginner.definition: An email account is a mailbox that a person uses to send and receive messages. If an attacker takes one over, the mailbox becomes a weapon. The attacker can read old messages and send new ones that look real. This detection looks for signs that a mailbox is being used by somebody other than its owner.
beginner.whyItMatters: Mail from a known colleague is trusted, so it bypasses most user suspicion. The attacker also gains password reset messages for other services, which can spread the compromise further. Internal mail is often the first step of an invoice fraud or a malware campaign. Detection is complicated because the sign in uses a real password. That is why the useful signals are the changes made inside the mailbox. Hidden forwarding rules and mail access from an unfamiliar program are two clear examples.
howItWorks: The mail service writes an audit record for each sign in, with the address, device and result.
It writes another record when a mailbox rule, forwarding address or permission changes.
The detection looks for a successful sign in from a new address followed by a mailbox change.
It also counts outbound messages per mailbox and compares the count with the normal pattern.
Password reset and multi factor authentication changes are added to the same timeline.
When several of these signals appear within a short time, the rule raises a high priority alert.
beginner.example: Think of a till receipt in a shop. The receipt alone does not prove a theft. But a receipt at three in the morning is a story. The till was opened with a manager card, and the refund went to a new bank account. Each line on the receipt is ordinary on its own. Together they describe something that should not happen. Your mail audit log works in the same way. A new sign in, a hidden forwarding rule and a burst of outbound messages form a story. A single event never shows that.
takeaways: A stolen mailbox is believed by everyone who trusts the person.
Watch the changes inside the mailbox, not only the sign in.
Hidden forwarding rules are one of the strongest signs of takeover.

objectives: Explain why attackers want to control a mailbox rather than only read it.
List the sign in and audit events that reveal mailbox abuse.
Correlate a sign in from a new location with mailbox configuration changes.
Set an outbound message volume threshold per mailbox group.
Describe the containment steps for a confirmed mailbox compromise.
dataSources: Mail or identity provider sign in logs with user, source address, client application and authentication result
Mailbox audit records for rule creation, forwarding address changes and mailbox permission grants
Message trace or mail gateway logs with sender mailbox, recipient count and delivery outcome
Multi factor authentication registration and reset records for the affected account
Identity protection or impossible travel alerts raised by the identity platform
logic: The pattern is a successful authentication to a mailbox from an unfamiliar source followed by a configuration change that hides activity or exports mail, and often by a jump in outbound message volume. The fields that must be correlated are the mailbox owner, the source address and its reputation, the client application used, the mailbox rule parameters such as redirect or forward targets, and the count of messages sent per hour. Benign cases include a user setting a forwarding rule before holiday, a new phone that changes the client identifier and marketing users who send large batches. The malicious case combines a new country or hosting provider address with an external forwarding destination and messages to recipients the user never contacts.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Mailbox Forwarding Rule Added After Sign In From New Address
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection_login:
#     event_type: 'sign_in'
#     result: 'success'
#     src_ip|not_in: 'known_user_addresses'
#   selection_rule:
#     operation:
#       - 'New-InboxRule'
#       - 'Set-Mailbox'
#     parameters|contains: 'RedirectTo'
#   filter_approved:
#     user|in: 'approved_forwarding_accounts'
#   condition: selection_login and selection_rule and not filter_approved
# level: high
falsePositives: Users who create a legitimate forwarding rule while travelling on holiday.
Shared mailboxes managed by an administrator from a new jump host.
Marketing or support teams that send a large batch of messages from one mailbox.
A mailbox migration tool that signs in from a cloud service address and changes mailbox settings.
tuningNotes: Baseline the source addresses and client applications used by each mailbox group, and add filters for approved forwarding accounts and for support teams that send in bulk. Scope the sign in branch to mailboxes with access to sensitive data, because bulk senders create noise. Keep the mailbox rule branch unscoped, since rule creation is rare and cheap to review. If you narrow the rule to privileged accounts only, you lose the common case where a normal user mailbox is used to phish colleagues, so leave a medium severity version running across all mailboxes.
